summary: Describes HZ, a format for exchanging files with a mix of Chinese and ASCII characters. The content is identical to an article the author wrote in 1989. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A way to mix Chinese and English in one plain text file, with special signs showing where one begins and the other ends.

questions: how to mix chinese and ascii in one file
how does hz escape sequence work
subtitle: A way to mix Chinese and English in one plain-text file

tldr.problem: Email and early text systems were designed for ASCII, but people needed to send files containing both Chinese characters and English text.
tldr.mechanism: HZ encodes Chinese characters (GB2312-80) as two-byte pairs and ASCII as single bytes, using escape sequences (~{ and ~}) to switch between ASCII and Chinese modes, all within a 7-bit safe format.
tldr.outcome: A simple, reversible encoding that keeps plain-English text readable and uses only 7-bit characters safe for email transmission.

today: HZ encoding remains widely used for Chinese text exchange, though modern systems increasingly support UTF-8 and other Unicode formats natively.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
Most computer systems in the early 1990s handled Chinese text in 8-bit codes, but electronic mail required 7-bit transmission. A generic binary-to-ASCII encoder was insufficient because there was no universal 8-bit standard for Chinese. HZ solves this by encoding text in 7-bit form, using the national Chinese standard GB (GuoBiao, or GB2312-80).

The format supports a file with arbitrary mix of Chinese characters and English text, making it ideal both for email and for terminal emulators that display and edit such files in real time.
sections.eli5: Old email could only send plain text with 7-bit characters, but computers stored Chinese as 8-bit pairs. HZ lets you write both in one message safely by switching modes with special markers.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
HZ operates in two modes. The default is ASCII mode, where each byte is a single ASCII character. When a tilde character (~) appears, it acts as an escape sequence: ~{ switches to GB mode, where characters are read two bytes at a time as GB codes. The sequence ~} switches back to ASCII mode. To write a literal tilde, use ~~. The sequence ~\n (tilde-newline) marks a line break without producing output, useful for fitting long lines within 80 characters.

This means a file containing only English stays readable as plain ASCII (except for the tilde, which is always written as ~~). A decoder needs to look ahead at most one character in the stream.
sections.eli5: ~{ means "everything coming now is Chinese pairs", ~} means "back to English", and ~~ means "I really want a tilde here".

sections.title: Encoding Examples
sections.content:
An English sentence stays unchanged: This sentence is in ASCII. To encode a mix, Chinese characters (in GB form) are wrapped: Here is English.~{<:Ky2;S{#,NpJ)l6HK!#~}Back to English. The RFC recommends keeping lines under 80 characters for compatibility with utilities like more, which means inserting ~} at line ends and resuming with ~{ on the next line when GB text spans multiple lines.

The beauty of HZ is that many different encoding styles can produce the same output, and a single decoder handles all of them.
sections.eli5: You write English normally, and when you need Chinese, you mark where it starts and stops with curly braces after a tilde.
